findings.issue: Source: "like children or widowed women, they murmur"; candidate: "they whine". "Whine" sharpens Butler's neutral "murmur".
findings.fix: “King Agamemnon, the Achaeans are about to make you a byword among all mankind. They have forgotten the promise they made you when they set out from Argos, that you would not return until you had sacked the town of Troy. Like children or widowed women, they murmur and want to set off for home. It is true that they have had toil enough to lose heart. A man grows restless at being away from his wife even for a single month, when he is on shipboard at the mercy of wind and sea. But we have now been kept here nine long years. So I cannot blame the Achaeans for turning restive. Still, we will be shamed if we go home empty-handed after so long a stay. Therefore, my friends, be patient a little longer, so that we may learn whether the prophecies of Calchas were false or true.

findings.issue: Source: "dwelt in ... rocky Calydon, for the great king Oeneus had now no sons living"; candidate splits the sentence and drops the causal "for" that explains why Thoas commands.
findings.fix: Thoas, son of Andraemon, commanded the Aetolians, who lived in Pleuron, Olenus, Pylene, Chalcis by the sea, and rocky Calydon, for the great king Oeneus now had no sons living and was himself dead, as was golden-haired Meleager, who had been set over the Aetolians as their king. Forty ships came with Thoas.

findings.issue: Source: "son of Admetus, whom Alcestis bore to him"; candidate: "Alcestis bore him to Admetus" is awkward and a general reader may misread who bore whom.
findings.fix: And those who held Pherae by the Boebean lake, with Boebe, Glaphyrae and the populous city of Iolcus, with their eleven ships, were led by Eumelus, son of Admetus, whom Alcestis bore to him. She was the loveliest of the daughters of Pelias.

findings.issue: Candidate: "The Enienes and the valiant Peraebi followed him, who lived around wintry Dodona"; the relative clause attaches to Guneus ("him"), whereas the source says the Enienes and Peraebi dwelt there.
findings.fix: Guneus brought twenty-two ships from Cyphus. The Enienes and the valiant Peraebi followed him. They lived around wintry Dodona and held the lands around the lovely river Titaresius, which sends its waters into the Peneus. The Titaresius does not mingle with the silver eddies of the Peneus but flows on top of them like oil, because it is a branch of dread Orcus and of the river Styx.

findings.issue: Source: "Adrestus and Amphius, whose breastplate was of linen" is ambiguous about whom it describes; candidate resolves it to Amphius alone ("Amphius wore a breastplate of linen").'

"peer of Jove in counsel" is rendered "the equal of Zeus in counsel" here but "peer of Zeus in counsel" at p47 (and "equal of the gods" at p26); "peer" is used for Ares at p46 and p49. Not in the STYLE-NOTE table; unify if desired.
Candidate adds the count "five captains"; Butler gives five names but no number. Harmless but technically an addition.
